passage:
When sociologists speak of a 'profession,' they usually mean more than simply a line of work in which someone earns a living. According to the sociologist Andrew Abbott, a profession is an occupation that has secured the exclusive right to perform a particular set of tasks and that controls entry into its own ranks through training, examination, and licensure. On this definition, medicine and law are the paradigm cases, while many other lines of work — including some that pay well and require long training — fall short of full professional status.

Abbott argues that what distinguishes a profession from an ordinary occupation is the social bargain it strikes with the wider public. In return for a monopoly over certain tasks, the profession agrees to police its own members: it sets standards of competence, disciplines those who fall short, and accepts the idea that the quality of its work is something only other members can reliably judge. The public, for its part, is relieved of the burden of evaluating practitioners one by one, since the license itself is meant to serve as a guarantee.

This arrangement, however, depends on conditions that are not always met. The self-policing on which the bargain rests can weaken when the profession's internal culture discourages frank criticism, or when the cost of expelling an incompetent member is felt to fall too heavily on colleagues who must testify against him. Abbott notes that complaints about professional misconduct are, in practice, often resolved quietly, in ways that protect the profession's public standing but leave the aggrieved client without redress. When such failures accumulate, the state may step in and replace professional self-regulation with outside review — a development that Abbott treats as evidence that the original bargain has broken down.

Even where self-regulation functions tolerably well, the professional model has critics. Some sociologists argue that the monopoly granted to a profession tends, over time, to serve the interests of its members more than those of the public it nominally serves, by restricting the supply of practitioners and keeping fees high. Abbott concedes that this risk is real but contends that the alternative — a system in which clients must evaluate complex technical work without reliable credentials — would leave most of them worse off. The case for professions, on his account, is not that they are free of self-interest but that the public is better served by regulated self-interest than by no regulation at all.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: According to Abbott, a profession is best understood as a social bargain in which an occupation's monopoly over certain tasks is exchanged for self-regulation that, though imperfect, serves the public better than no regulation at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medicine and law are the only occupations that fully satisfy Abbott's definition of a profession, since no other line of work has secured a comparable monopoly over its tasks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Professional self-regulation has broken down so thoroughly in most fields that state review has become the standard means of disciplining incompetent practitioners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The principal value of the professional model is that it restricts the supply of practitioners, thereby guaranteeing that those who remain are highly competent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sociologists who study professions disagree fundamentally about whether professional licensure benefits the public or merely entrenches the interests of licensed practitioners.

explanations.correct: The passage defines professions through Abbott's bargain (paragraph 1-2), notes when the bargain breaks down (paragraph 3), addresses critics (paragraph 4), and closes with Abbott's qualified defense. A captures both the bargain and Abbott's verdict.
explanations.B: Too narrow: medicine and law are called paradigm cases, not the only professions.
explanations.C: Overstated: state review is described as an occasional corrective, not the standard practice.
explanations.D: Confuses a criticism (restricted supply) with the author's case for professions.
explanations.E: The passage reports disagreement but its main point is Abbott's own position, not that disagreement exists.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A definition is offered; the terms of a social bargain are laid out; conditions under which the bargain can fail are described; a criticism is noted and answered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing definitions of a profession are compared; one is shown to be superior on empirical grounds; its implications for public policy are drawn out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A puzzle about professional licensure is posed; several historical examples are surveyed; a new explanation of the puzzle is defended.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A recent criticism of the professional model is introduced; the response of its defenders is summarized; the dispute is declared unresolved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A classification scheme is proposed; its application to medicine and law is illustrated; its application to other occupations is left for future research.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines; paragraph 2 lays out the bargain; paragraph 3 describes conditions under which it fails; paragraph 4 raises a criticism and gives Abbott's answer. A tracks each move.
explanations.B: Only one definition — Abbott's — is presented.
explanations.C: No puzzle is posed and no historical survey is offered.
explanations.D: The dispute is not declared unresolved; Abbott's qualified case closes the passage.
explanations.E: No classification scheme with multiple categories is proposed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Abbott treats the intervention of the state to replace professional self-regulation as

choices.label: A
choices.text: the normal means by which all professions are ultimately disciplined

choices.label: B
choices.text: evidence that the bargain between the profession and the public has broken down

choices.label: C
choices.text: a development that the profession itself typically welcomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: proof that the professional model was never workable in the first place

choices.label: E
choices.text: an outcome that tends to lower standards of competence within the profession

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that outside review by the state is treated by Abbott 'as evidence that the original bargain has broken down.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier: the passage presents state review as an occasional corrective, not the normal means.
explanations.C: Plausible-world fact the passage never supplies.
explanations.D: Overreach: breakdown of the bargain in some cases is not proof that the model was never workable.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the passage does not claim outside review lowers standards.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that, under the professional bargain as Abbott describes it, the public is

choices.label: A
choices.text: expected to rely on the license as a guarantee of a practitioner's competence

choices.label: B
choices.text: invited to participate directly in disciplining incompetent practitioners

choices.label: C
choices.text: guaranteed redress whenever professional misconduct occurs

choices.label: D
choices.text: charged with setting the standards of competence that the profession must meet

choices.label: E
choices.text: required to evaluate each practitioner's qualifications individually

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 says the public is relieved of evaluating practitioners one by one because 'the license itself is meant to serve as a guarantee.'
explanations.B: Reverses the passage: disciplining is done by the profession, not the public.
explanations.C: Altered qualifier: paragraph 3 notes that aggrieved clients are often left without redress.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: the profession sets standards.
explanations.E: Reverses the passage: the point of licensure is precisely to spare the public this task.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that Abbott would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A line of work that is demanding and well compensated automatically qualifies as a profession in the sociological sense.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fact that professionals sometimes act in their own interest shows that the professional model should be abandoned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Self-regulation by a profession can be imperfect and still leave the public better off than a system in which clients must evaluate technical work on their own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complaints of professional misconduct are generally handled in a way that fully satisfies the clients who bring them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The monopoly granted to a profession produces no benefit for its members beyond the prestige of the title.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 gives Abbott's case: the professional model is not free of self-interest, but 'the public is better served by regulated self-interest than by no regulation at all.' C restates that hedged position.
explanations.A: Reverses paragraph 1: even well-paid, long-trained work may fall short of professional status.
explanations.B: Overreach: Abbott concedes self-interest is real but defends the model, not abandons it.
explanations.D: Reverses paragraph 3: complaints are often resolved in ways that leave aggrieved clients without redress.
explanations.E: The passage says monopoly restricts supply and keeps fees high, which is a benefit to members, not none.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of the observation that complaints of professional misconduct are often resolved quietly serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a way in which the conditions needed for professional self-regulation to work can fail

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that Abbott's definition of a profession is empirically inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a new category of occupations that do not yet qualify as professions

choices.label: D
choices.text: support the claim that the state should always oversee professional discipline

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that the public has no interest in how professions discipline their members

explanations.correct: The observation appears in paragraph 3 as an example of how the self-policing on which the bargain depends 'is not always met.' Its rhetorical function is illustrative.
explanations.B: Wrong function: the observation describes a failure mode, not a flaw in the definition.
explanations.C: The passage introduces no new category at this point.
explanations.D: Overstated: the passage describes state review as an occasional corrective, not something that should always occur.
explanations.E: Opposite of the passage, which treats the public as the principal beneficiary of the bargain.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Abbott's account of professions can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified enthusiasm for its conclusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: respectful presentation of a position the author finds defensible

choices.label: C
choices.text: open hostility to its central claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality between Abbott and his critics

choices.label: E
choices.text: reluctant agreement with its critics despite the author's preference for Abbott

explanations.correct: The author reports Abbott's definition, gives space to its difficulties, and allows Abbott's qualified case to close the passage — the posture of respectful presentation.
explanations.A: Overstated: the author does not speak enthusiastically and notes real difficulties.
explanations.C: Opposite of the text, which treats Abbott seriously.
explanations.D: Too weak: the passage is not evenhanded; it lets Abbott have the last word.
explanations.E: Reverses the passage, which gives Abbott, not the critics, the closing position.

passage:
Until fairly recently, the rapid growth of cities in the nineteenth-century United States was commonly explained in simple terms: factories, it was said, drew workers from the countryside, and cities grew up around the factories. According to the urban historian Sam Bass Warner, however, this factory-first account misses much of what actually happened. Drawing on street directories, tax records, and transit maps, Warner argues that the most important engine of nineteenth-century urban growth was not the factory but the streetcar, and that the typical American city of the period expanded outward from its old commercial core in ways that had little to do with where the largest employers were located.

Warner's evidence comes chiefly from Boston, where, between roughly 1870 and 1900, the introduction of horse-drawn and then electric streetcar lines made it possible for clerks, shopkeepers, and skilled tradesmen to live several miles from the places at which they worked. As new lines pushed outward into formerly rural towns, small builders bought up inexpensive land along the route, subdivided it into narrow lots, and put up modest wooden houses for sale to families of modest means. The result was a ring of new residential neighborhoods, each one organized around a streetcar stop rather than a factory gate.

The significance of this pattern, Warner argues, is that it reshaped the social geography of the city. Under the older, walking-distance arrangement, rich and poor had lived close together, since everyone needed to be near the center. Once the streetcar made distance cheap, those who could afford the daily fare moved outward, and the inner districts were left to the poorest residents and to the workshops and warehouses that served the downtown economy. The familiar twentieth-century pattern of a poor urban core surrounded by wealthier suburbs, Warner suggests, was already visible in outline by 1900.

Warner's account has been refined by later historians, who have shown that factories did matter in some cities — Pittsburgh and Detroit among them — and that the streetcar's reach depended on local politics and the willingness of city governments to grant franchises. Still, his central insight has held up well. For a broad class of American cities, the shape of nineteenth-century urban growth is better explained by transit than by industry, and any account of the period that begins with the factory alone will miss the new suburbs that the streetcar, more than any factory whistle, called into being.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For a broad class of American cities, the nineteenth-century expansion into new residential neighborhoods is better explained by the spread of streetcar lines than by the location of factories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sam Bass Warner's work on Boston shows that horse-drawn and electric streetcar lines were introduced in that city between roughly 1870 and 1900.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nineteenth-century American cities grew because small builders purchased inexpensive rural land and subdivided it into narrow lots for modest wooden houses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factories played no meaningful role in the growth of any nineteenth-century American city, despite the views of earlier historians.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The twentieth-century pattern of poor urban cores surrounded by wealthier suburbs was entirely produced by public transit decisions made before 1900.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the factory-first view, replaces it with Warner's streetcar account, draws out the social consequences, and closes with the hedged conclusion that 'for a broad class of American cities, the shape of nineteenth-century urban growth is better explained by transit than by industry.' A tracks that thesis.
explanations.B: Too narrow: a single detail, not the passage's thesis.
explanations.C: Too narrow: a mechanism of growth, not the claim the passage is making about explanations.
explanations.D: Overstated: paragraph 4 explicitly concedes that factories did matter in Pittsburgh and Detroit.
explanations.E: Overstated: the passage says the pattern was 'already visible in outline by 1900,' not entirely produced by 1900.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under the walking-distance arrangement that preceded the streetcar,

choices.label: A
choices.text: factories were concentrated at the edges of the city rather than in the center

choices.label: B
choices.text: rich and poor residents tended to live close to one another, since everyone needed to be near the center

choices.label: C
choices.text: most residents lived in rural towns and traveled daily into the city for work

choices.label: D
choices.text: small builders had already begun to subdivide suburban land in anticipation of transit improvements

choices.label: E
choices.text: city governments declined to grant franchises to private transportation companies

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that 'under the older, walking-distance arrangement, rich and poor had lived close together, since everyone needed to be near the center.'
explanations.A: The passage does not locate factories at the edges under the older arrangement.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage: the streetcar, not the walking city, enabled daily travel from outside.
explanations.D: Out of scope: builders' subdivision activity is tied to streetcar expansion, not the pre-streetcar period.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the franchise question is raised only as a later qualification of Warner's account.

questions.questionStem: The passage indicates that Warner drew his evidence chiefly from which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pittsburgh and Detroit

choices.label: B
choices.text: A comparative study of a dozen industrial cities

choices.label: C
choices.text: Boston, between roughly 1870 and 1900

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interviews with nineteenth-century streetcar operators

choices.label: E
choices.text: Records of factory employment in the northeastern United States

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that 'Warner's evidence comes chiefly from Boston, where, between roughly 1870 and 1900,' the streetcar network was built out.
explanations.A: Pittsburgh and Detroit are mentioned as counterexamples by later historians, not as Warner's evidence.
explanations.B: The passage does not describe Warner's work as a comparative study of many cities.
explanations.D: Plausible-world fact the passage never supplies; Warner's sources are given as directories, tax records, and transit maps.
explanations.E: Factory-employment records are not among the sources the passage credits to Warner.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Pittsburgh and Detroit serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the typical pattern of streetcar-driven residential growth

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualify Warner's account by acknowledging cities in which factories did matter

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the cities from which Warner drew his principal evidence

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that later historians have generally failed to improve on Warner's account

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that the factory-first explanation has no empirical basis anywhere

explanations.correct: The reference appears in paragraph 4, where later historians 'have shown that factories did matter in some cities — Pittsburgh and Detroit among them.' Its function is to qualify, not to overturn, Warner's account.
explanations.A: Wrong function: these cities are cited as exceptions to Warner's pattern, not illustrations of it.
explanations.C: Confuses Warner's evidence (Boston) with the later qualifying examples.
explanations.D: Opposite of the passage, which says Warner's central insight has held up well.
explanations.E: Overstated: the reference shows the factory-first view has some application, not that it is wholly baseless.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that Warner would agree with which one of the following statements about nineteenth-century American cities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city's pattern of residential growth in this period cannot be understood without some attention to how its inhabitants moved around.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factories played no role in shaping the neighborhoods of any American city in this period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The social segregation of rich and poor that appears in twentieth-century cities is unrelated to nineteenth-century transit decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Street directories and tax records are not reliable sources for urban historians working on the period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The development of suburban neighborhoods in this period was essentially the work of city governments rather than private builders.

explanations.correct: Warner's whole case — drawn from transit maps and neighborhood growth — rests on the importance of how people moved through the city. A is a hedged statement he would plainly accept.
explanations.B: Overreach: Warner's qualifier about Pittsburgh and Detroit shows he would not deny factories any role.
explanations.C: Contradicts paragraph 3, which ties twentieth-century segregation directly to nineteenth-century transit.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: these are the sources on which Warner himself relies.
explanations.E: Reverses paragraph 2: small private builders, not city governments, developed the new neighborhoods.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Warner's account can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: broadly approving, while acknowledging that later historians have refined it

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissive, on the grounds that it ignores the role of factories

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic, without reservation of any kind

choices.label: D
choices.text: skeptical, because the evidence is drawn from a single city

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral, since the author takes no position between Warner and his critics

explanations.correct: The author presents Warner's case at length, notes that later historians have added qualifications, and concludes that Warner's 'central insight has held up well.' A captures the mixed-but-positive posture.
explanations.B: Opposite of the passage, which endorses Warner's insight.
explanations.C: Overstated: the author explicitly records the qualifications of later historians.
explanations.D: Wrong direction: the author accepts Warner despite the Boston focus.
explanations.E: Too weak: the final paragraph's closing sentence is clearly on Warner's side.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support Warner's claim that streetcar expansion, rather than factory location, drove the residential growth of typical nineteenth-century American cities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In several cities other than Boston, new residential neighborhoods formed in the late nineteenth century were consistently organized around streetcar stops rather than around industrial sites.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In Pittsburgh and Detroit, factory employment grew substantially between 1870 and 1900.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Street directories from nineteenth-century Boston are the most detailed records of their kind to survive from the period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electric streetcar replaced the horse-drawn streetcar in most American cities during the 1890s.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some nineteenth-century city governments granted streetcar franchises only after long political disputes.

explanations.correct: Warner's claim is general: transit, not industry, shaped the typical residential pattern. Direct evidence from other cities showing the same transit-centered pattern most strongly supports that generalization.
explanations.B: Off-target: growth of factory employment in the atypical cities the passage already concedes does not support Warner's generalization.
explanations.C: Concerns the quality of one source, not whether the claim generalizes beyond Boston.
explanations.D: A technological detail that does not speak to the causal claim the question targets.
explanations.E: Concerns political conditions for streetcar franchises, not whether they, rather than factories, drove residential growth.
